Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: Council will generate income outside of rates and grants from rental, fees and charges, property sales, developer contributions and user fees and charges. Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: Council has maintained stability over the years against this ratio to support community outcomes where services are most needed.

Variation: Bass Coast Shire has one aquatic facility. Four health inspections were completed in the 2023/24 financial year.

Variation: Council's reporting framework did not allow reporting on number of days between receipt of animal management requests and first response action this financial year. This has since been resolved for future years.

Variation: The overall direct cost of the animal management service increase is primarily attributed to an increase in Officer's patrolling and providing service to the community.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: All ten animal management prosecutions in 2023/24 were successful.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: In 2023/24 Council received and investigated twenty food complaints.

Description: Cost of food safety service

Description: Food safety samples
Variation: Council obtained  91 food samples from food businesses for analysis which was above the required number of 86 food samples to be analysed.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: During 2023/24, 10 of 105 decisions were considered at closed meetings of Council. In comparison, 5 of 183 decisions were considered at closed meetings in 2022/23. Closed decisions include personnel and contractual matters.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Bass Coast Council community satisfaction rating for consultation and engagement has decreased by two points from the previous year and remains on par with other Large Rural Councils.

Variation: Council expenses increased in 2023/24 due to the expenses incurred for the recruitment of a new CEO.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions

Description: Library visits per head of population
Variation: In 2023/24, there was a total of 225,013 visits to the libraries located within the Bass Coast Shire.

Variation: Council does not have operational control of a MCH service

Variation: Council maintains 608.09 kilometres of sealed local roads. We received a total of 71 sealed local road requests in 2023/2024 compared to 81 requests in 2022/23.

Variation: In 2023/24 there were 608.09 kilometres of sealed local roads with 566.27 kilometres below Councils intervention level. For 2022/23 there were 602 kilometres of sealed local roads with 590 kilometres below Councils intervention level.

Variation: Council's pavement reconstruction costs have increased per square metre from $111.64 to $125.73 due to an increased proportion of urban road reconstruction from the previous year.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: In 2023/24 Council resealed 58,179.80 square metres of sealed local roads compared to 69,830 square metres in 2022/23. There has been an increase in the cost per square metre from $12.73 in 2022/23 to $13.25 in 2023/24.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: The Community Satisfaction score of 50 is a one point decrease on last years result, twelve points higher than the average for Large Rural Councils and five points higher than the State-wide average. It is important to note that the survey results are also a reflection of the state controlled roads within the municipality.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: Council continues to improve the updated software system and monitors the accuracy of numbers reported.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: The total number of planning applications for 2023/24 remained high. Throughout 2023/24 the team has continued to work through the challenges of the implementation of the new software system which has impacted the completion rate of planning application decisions.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The slight increase in the direct cost of the statutory planning service compared to the previous year is due to an increased number of complex VCAT applications and a reduced number of applications received, which is understandable given the current broader development industry context.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: Of the 468 planning applications in 2023/24 there were 22 VCAT decisions. VCAT upheld twenty Council decisions and two were set aside.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: For every 10,000 bins collected in Bass Coast, 2.7 are missed. All reported missed bins are collected the next day.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The 4.4% increase in cost of kerbside garbage collection is primarily due to inflationary pressures affecting third party kerbside collection costs.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: The 0.6% increase in cost of kerbside recycling is primarily due to inflationary pressures effecting third party kerbside collection costs.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The 1% decrease in total material collected, and 0.39% decrease in material diverted from landfill are consistent with the introduction of the Victorian Container Deposit Scheme from 1 November 2023.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: The 6.0 per cent increase is due to a 10 per cent increase in depreciation, and the delivery of additional operational projects.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: The 3.22 per cent increase in average rates per property assessment reflects a combination of the 3.50 per cent rate cap and the development of vacant land.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: This indicator has been impacted by a reduction in cash balances and deferred income as a result of capital works delivery. The target and 2024/25 forecast increase are due to a short term loan being refinanced long-term.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The decrease in this indicator in 2023/24 is due to funds held in term deposits with original maturities greater than 90 days of $36.6 million being classed as other financial assets instead of cash. These cash balances are included as cash in Council’s forecast. Treating the $36.6 million as unrestricted cash would result in the indicator being 64.73%.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: During 2023/24 Council drew down on borrowings for construction of intergenerational projects, this will continue during the forward outlook.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: A short-term loan rollover ($8 million) has been accounted for as a repayment and redraw in each financial year. In 2023/24 this redraw was increased to $12.57 million, with future year end predictions based on extended loan terms.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: The decrease in this indicator in 2023/24 is due to an increase in Council’s own source revenue and reclassification of some loan balances as current. Increases from 2024/25 and onward is due to the planned draw down of borrowings which will fund the delivery of intergenerational projects.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: Council has accelerated its capital works delivery and is now renewing and upgrading its assets in line with its asset management plans.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: Council's underlying result has been impacted by the delayed receipt of $8.8 million in funding from the Victorian Grants Commission. In previous years this funding had been received in advance. Treating the $8.8 million as received would result in the indicator being -3.28%.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: Council continues to have a high reliance on rate revenue consistent with other large rural Council’s.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: The increase experienced in 2023/24 is due to an overall 0.64 percent decrease in capital improved property values within the municipality and 3.5% rates increase.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: The 2023/24 increase of 5.17 per cent is attributable to increases in depreciation and borrowing costs.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: The value of Council’s infrastructure has increased in 2023/24 because of; Fair value infrastructure revaluation ($267 million) Capital works expenditure ($36 million) and developer contributed assets ($16 million).

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: The continuous increase in population has resulted in higher population density per length of road.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: The 2023/24 increase is due to additional revenue associated with the operation of Berninneit through bookings and ticket sales and improved financial returns due to a higher interest rate environment.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: Increase in recurrent grants in 2021/22 and 2022/23 is due to increased Victorian Grants Commission funding received in advance. This revenue stream was not received in advance in the 2023/24 financial year.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The socio-economic disadvantage index is prepared by the ABS. The result is based on a scale of one for most disadvantaged and ten for least disadvantaged.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: Staff turnover has been consistent in prior years and shows a small increase in 2023/24. Council’s turnover is on par with industry average.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The cost of the library service increased by 1.11% from 2022/23. During this period, the Bass Coast population increased by 2.37% resulting in a minor decrease in costs per population.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council Officers completed required inspections of all Council owned aquatic facilities.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation:
In total, there were 391,401 visits to Council aquatic facilities in 2023/24. This is approximately 26,000 less visits than last year. 

Despite this reduction, the number of visits per person remains comparable to last year's result of 7.1.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: Energy pricing was a major driver in the the cost of service delivery increasing this year. Contract variations and venue operating costs were also contributing factors. This, combined with lower attendance rates resulted in a cost of $4.40 per visit.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation:
Customer response times have reduced from 4.3 days in 2021/22, to 1.3 days this year. Improvement initiatives from the previous year continue to have a positive impact. 

The reduction in response times is a significant result, considering that the number of animal management requests received has increased by 45 percent, from 2,160 last year to 3,140 this year.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation:
The number of collected animals reduced by 21 percent, from 605 last year to 478 this year. This indicates that the responsible pet ownership program in its second year of delivery continues to have a positive impact. 

The total percentage of animals reclaimed continues to increase.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation:
Council continues to actively work on improving the rehoming rate of unclaimed animals. The total animals rehomed or reclaimed throughout the year was 88 percent (424 animals).

A mandated change in the calculation of this measure has also contributed to the significant increase. From this year on, reclaimed animals have been removed from this measure to give a more accurate reflection of animals rehomed.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation:
The total cost for the animal management service decreased by approximately $80,000 this year, equating to a cost of $15.30 per head of the population.

The cost of this service includes activities such as compliance, management of the Municipal Animal Pound, and veterinary services.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation:
There were 16 animal management prosecutions this year (increasing from five last year). All were successfully pursued by Council.  

Prosecutions are conducted on an as needs basis or when required under the Domestic Animals Act 1994. Council’s primary strategy remains focused on community safety, communication, education, and promotion of responsible pet ownership.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Consistent with previous years, most complaints were responded to within 24 hours. Council responded to 33 complaints this year.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation:
Council aims to complete all required annual food safety assessments for registered Class 1 and 2 food premises. 

Council completed 306 assessments this year, representing 94 percent of the target. Assessments not completed were largely due to some premises only opening for short periods during the year due to seasonality of their trade.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: The service cost reduced to previous levels this year and equated to $255 per premises. There was a higher number of registered premises this year (1,170) compared to last year (933) which contributed to a lower cost per premises.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: During the year, there were a total of 29 critical and major non-compliance notifications, all of which were followed up by Council.

Description: Food safety samples
Variation:
Council collected 85 samples throughout the year, one more than the required 84.

As this is a new measure from 2023/24 there are no comparative results available.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: Council decisions made during meetings closed to the public returned to previous levels. The higher result last year was caused by Tender Recommendations and Acquisitions defined as confidential under the Local Government Act 2020.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation:
Satisfaction with consultation and engagement decreased by one point compared to the previous year. The average result for similar sized Councils was 48. 

Note: 2022 result was incorrectly reported as 53, the actual result was 51.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Councillor attendance at Council meetings across the financial year was slightly lower but still consistent with previous years.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation:
The cost of elected representation includes Councillor allowances, the cost of travel to meetings to advocate to State and Federal Governments, the cost of mandatory Councillor induction, the cost of training, professional development, catering, and IT expenses. 
Council’s commitment to advocacy has increased the cost of travel for this financial year.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Satisfaction with Council making decisions in the interest of the community decreased by three points compared to the previous year. The average result for similar sized Councils was 46.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation:
There were 57,136 items in the library collection (including e-resources) with 38,836 of those items being purchased in the last five years. 

The proportion of the library collection that is less than five years old was consistent with previous years.

Description: Loans per head of population
Variation:
There were over 198,000 loans made during the year, which equates to 3.27 loans per item. The total number of loans is consistent with last year's result.

As this is a new measure from 2023/24 there are no comparative results available.

Description: Library membership
Variation:
There were 18,810 registered library members at the end of the 2023/24 year. This number equates to 31 percent of the municipal population.

As this is a new measure from 2023/24 there are no comparative results available.

Description: Library visits per head of population
Variation:
There were approximately 139,000 visits to Council libraries during the year, equating to over two visits per resident.

As this is a new measure from 2023/24 there are no comparative results available.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation:
All birth notifications received were actioned and all newborns were enrolled in Council’s Maternal and Child Health Service. During the year, 744 infants were enrolled in the service.

The result is more than 100 percent because babies born late in the previous year participated in the service this financial year.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation:
Council provided over 16,000 hours of Maternal and Child Health Services for families during the year, resulting in a cost of $86.65 per hour of service. 

Council provided more than 1,000 extra hours this year with only a small increase in the total cost of service. This resulted in a reduced hourly cost of service.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: The overall participation rate for the Maternal and Child Health Service was 67 percent, which is marginally lower than the previous financial year.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Participation in the Maternal and Child Health service by Aboriginal children was 72 percent and is marginally higher than previous years.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: The service received 734 birth notices during the year and conducted 689 four-week Key Age and Stage assessments.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Council received a lower number of customer requests compared to last year. High rainfall and severe storm events continue to impact the volume of requests received by Council. Response times have improved, with requests now being inspected and addressed within an average of 3.4 days.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation:
Council continued to maintain a high proportion of its road network to the condition standards. 

Road condition was modelled on historical data as condition assessments are completed every four years.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: Council continues to investigate and utilise materials that increase the longevity of our roads. As a result, Council increased the volume of asphalt used this year. This coupled with increasing cost of materials and the impact of inclement weather conditions have increased the result for this measure.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: Council increased investment this year in preparatory works to improve longevity of roads in the network. This coupled with increasing cost of materials and the impact of inclement weather conditions have increased the result for this measure.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Satisfaction with sealed local roads decreased by three points compared to the previous year. The average result for similar sized Councils was 38.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: The time taken to decide planning applications decreased this year. This is a positive result stemming from Council's sustained focus on reducing the backlog of historical applications with long processing times.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: The percentage of planning applications decided within the required timeframes continues to improve and is attributed to process improvements and workforce stability.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The total cost of the planning service decreased by approximately $162,000 compared to last year, however the lower number of applications received by Council (395 for the year) has caused the cost per application to increase.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation:
The decrease in the result compared to last financial year is due to an increase in VCAT cases being settled prior to the formal hearing.

A change in State reporting guidelines has resulted in cases that were struck out, settled or withdrawn not being included in the results, which in the past has added to more positive results.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation:
There was a total of 182, or 0.9 bins missed for every 10,000 scheduled kerbside garbage and recycling bin lifts. 

Despite an increase in the total number of bins collected for the year, 33 percent less bins were missed.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The cost of kerbside garbage collection remains consistent with last year at $154 per bin. Service cost has increased over the previous two years due to the landfill levy, labour, fuel, population growth, and transportation costs.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: Both the cost of the recycling bin service and the number of bins increased marginally over the year, however, Council was able to maintain a consistent cost compared to previous years.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The landfill diversion rate for this year remained consistent with previous years. More than half of the waste collected was recycled or processed for green organics.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation:
The actual result is consistent with last year.

The target result did not allow for the $5.6 million natural disaster rectification cost (mostly funded from the state government cost recovery) or the $4.9 million transfer of capital expenditure (funded from capital budget) to materials and services. Additionally, Council incurred an asset write-off of $2.1 million as part of asset renewal. The total unplanned expenditure of $12.6 million, partly funded through the capital budget, state grants, and assets, led to an increase in total expenditure, resulting in a higher cost per assessment compared to the target position.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: This result is consistent with last year.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation:
Council's current asset balance reduced mainly due to decreased cash and term deposit balances. Some of the term deposits are classified as non-current assets due to their terms. This reduction in current assets, along with an increase in current liabilities due to loan refinancing, and the drawdown of a new loan has impacted the overall balance.

However, the amount of funds in term deposits is sufficient for the Council to meet its obligations.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation:
The indicator excludes term deposits worth $49 million from unrestricted cash, in which Council invests most of its funds to maximise returns.  

The amount of funds in term deposits are sufficient for Council to meet its obligations.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council drew down a planned borrowing of $6.5 million for the extension of the Warragul Leisure Centre capital works. This was approved budgeted borrowing, leading to increased loan borrowings and a change in the ratio.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation:
Council has arranged funding on a short-term basis due to the current interest rate environment, resulting in the payment of loans that were refinanced for an extended short term, leading to an increase in the variance percentage.

During 2023/24, Council refinanced $8 million and borrowed an additional $6.5 million. This indicates Council’s ability to meet debt commitments from rate revenue. In the forecasted years, we expect to refinance the loans on a long-term basis.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation:
Council's refinance of loan facilities for a shorter period of time resulted in reclassification of non current liability to current liability.
Council's non currently liability reduced from $22.5m in 2022/23 to $18.3m in 2023/24, which was the main driver for the variance movement.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation:
Council's renewal and upgrade expenditure was in line with the budget and asset requirements. Due to delays in capital projects and expenditure not meeting the capital thresholds, capital expenditure was lower in 2022/23.
The future year percentage is based on the 2024/25 Council Long Term Infrastructure Plan, which assumes the projects to be completed on time.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: The Financial Assistance Grant for 2024 was paid in advance in 2022/23, resulting in an unfavourable variance of $12 million. In addition, Council had unexpected expenditures relating to storm damage rectification and capital expenditure not meeting the asset capitalisation definition. This resulted in a transfer to operating ($5 million) and Asset write off as a part of capitalisation ($2 million) and was the main cause of the variance.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: The increase in variance for 2023/24 reflects Council’s genuine reliance on rates revenue as a primary source of income.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: This result is consistent with last year.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: This result is consistent with last year.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: This result is consistent with last year.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: Council manages a local road network of 1,829 kilometres, resulting in a ratio of 33 people for each kilometre of local road.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: This result is consistent with last year.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: Financial Assistance Grants (a main component of recurrent grants) were paid in advance in 2022/23, resulting in a significant reduction of funds. This led to a reduction of funds per head of municipal population.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) prepares an index of relative socio-economic disadvantage. The result for the municipality is six, where one is the most, and ten is the least disadvantaged.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation:
Percentage of staff turnover decreased for the second year in a row. 

The increase in 2021/22 was primarily attributed to Council's exit of the Aged and Disability Services.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The cost of delivering the library service is consistent with previous years.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council owns two aquatic facilities in Bayside: Sandringham Leisure Centre and Middle Brighton Sea Baths which are managed under private commercial lease and agreements. Council is not responsible for the operation or management of the Sandringham Aquatic Centre and the Middle Brighton Sea Bath is not technically defined as an aquatic facility.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council owns two aquatic facilities in Bayside: Sandringham Leisure Centre and Middle Brighton Sea Baths which are managed under private commercial lease and agreements. Council is not responsible for the operation or management of the Sandringham Aquatic Centre and the Middle Brighton Sea Bath is not technically defined as an aquatic facility.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: Council owns two aquatic facilities in Bayside: Sandringham Leisure Centre and Middle Brighton Sea Baths which are managed under private commercial lease and agreements. Council is not responsible for the operation or management of the Sandringham Aquatic Centre and the Middle Brighton Sea Bath is not technically defined as an aquatic facility.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: An increase in time taken is related to an increase in the number of requests due to all animal administration requests now being included into the total calculation of animal requests actioned. Another contributing factor is staff resourcing challenges and a vacancy.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: The number of animals reclaimed remains higher than the historic average of similar Councils.  This is attributed to a high portion of animals being registered, Council’s efforts to reunite collected animals before impounding and our community’s care for their pets.  The drop in claimed animals is offset by an increase in rehomed animals and may be attributed to the uptake in pet ownership during the pandemic.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: The percentage of collected animals rehomed has experienced an increase from previous years however the number of animals available for rehoming is low with 30 animals comprising 10 dogs and 20 cats.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: Continued focus on efficiency of service means the cost remains stable and within budget. The cost is similar to previous years and close to average for similar metropolitan councils.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: Council’s commitment to responsible pet ownership is reinforced though a range of education programs, communications and officer patrols along with taking enforcement action consistent with the Domestic Animals Act 1994. Serious matters warranting prosecution are pursued accordingly for both specific and general deterrence. The 100% success rate reflects the high quality of officers’ investigations and Council’s willingness to act.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: Council responded to 41 complaints in 58 days. The lower number of complaints received in the reporting year in comparison to previous years has assisted in enabling continued improvement in time taken to respond.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: Definition of assessment was altered to include only specific businesses carrying out high risk practices. Therefore only 85 businesses in Bayside were impacted, and all 85 received a food safety assessment. However Council inspected all class 1 and 2 businesses resulting in 562 food safety assessments conducted of 562 premises in 2023, consistent with previous years.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: Cost of the food service is slightly higher than last year, but consistent with previous years, and below the average for metropolitan councils. The slight increase is due to paying for agency Health Officers, to cover staff vacancies for an extended period.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: Major and critical non compliances continue to be a high priority. Environmental Health Officers ensure that all major and critical issues identified during the assessment period are followed up as a priority  within the required timeframes to mitigate the risks to community.

Description: Food safety samples
Variation: Council collected all food samples (138) as required under the Government Gazette.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: The number of decisions made at meetings closed to the public continues  to be low (12/342), despite a slight increase on the previous year. The figure remains below the average for similar councils.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: The satisfaction rating is sourced from the annual satisfaction survey conducted by an independent research company. Council continues to use diverse methods to communicate and engage with the community. This may have contributed to the minor increase in satisfaction that is well above that of similar councils.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Bayside continues to demonstrate a good attendance of Councillors at council meetings well within the expected range and consistent with or marginally better than similar councils.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The cost of elected representation has increased and relates to statutory increase in Councillor allowances as awarded by the Victorian Independent Remuneration Tribunal (Tribunal), plus an increase in internet and mobile phone costs, and professional development for some compulsory training.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: The satisfaction rating is sourced from the annual satisfaction survey conducted by an independent research company. The result shows a minor increase in satisfaction. The rating is well above that of similar councils.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: This favourable increase in items less than 5 years old reflects the increase in e-resources purchased, matching community needs. The scope of including e-resources in this metric reflects the true picture of the purchasing trend over the last 5 years.

Description: Loans per head of population
Variation: The high number of loans per population, reflects the number of active borrowers in the Bayside municipality and is consistent with a user study that indicates that 80% of visitors come to borrow library items.

Description: Library membership
Variation: Several contributing factors have helped to see this pleasing increase in active members. Improved access to collections through our e-product catalogue and a new collection initiative of The Library of Things have contributed to the increase in active members. Independent research has shown that Bayside is a community of readers which is reflected in the strong number of active borrowers using our libraries.

Description: Library visits per head of population
Variation: This is a new metric, so trend data is unavailable, but is consistent with similar data capture analysed previously which indicating a steady increase after the pandemic impact when libraries were closed.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: The 100% percentage of infants enrolled in the MCH service reflects a continuing high level of community satisfaction with the service.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: The Maternal and Child Health (MCH) service provides support and information to families with children from birth to school age who live in the municipality. The cost of the MCH service is consistent with last financial year.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Participation of 84.53% is a strong result. Participation rates have remained stable and continues to reflect high community satisfaction with the service.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Participation rates are strong and have remained stable which continues to reflect high community satisfaction with the service. Participation was 100% in the 0-3 year old cohort, and declined in the 3-5 year old cohort.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Defined as the percentage of infants enrolled in the MCH service who participated in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit. Participation is high in Bayside. In 2023/24 the percentage is > 100% as families move into the Bayside LGA after the birth of their child in another LGA.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: The number of road requests has returned to a number consistent with previous trend, after a spike in 2022/23 due to significant rain and flooding in that year that impacted local road conditions.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Council's pavement management system and Geographic Information System (GIS) provide timely data capture on road condition, enabling an accurate response so that Council meets the target of 97% for all local roads maintained to standard.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: The minimal costs expended in this and prior years are carried forward in preparation for works that were delayed to 2025 to align with work being done by utility providers.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: Expenditure consistent with previous year trends. It has reduced slightly on 2022/23 following increased levels of treatment required in that year.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: The community satisfaction has dropped slightly. Some of this is due to high levels of work being done on state owned arterial roads, and works being done by utilities. Council is advocating and consulting on an ongoing basis to those third parties to ensure that roads are managed and returned to council approved standards. Council’s day to day local road management is the same as previous years.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: The median processing time is based on the total calendar days it takes to assess an application. The improved times reflect a continued focus on processing efficiency within our statutory planning service. This is a strong result substantially lower than the metropolitan average.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: Bayside has sustained a high percentage of applications processed within the statutory timeframe above our target of 75%. A slight decrease over quarter 2 and 3 was experienced due to implications associated with the Victorian Government planning reforms.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: Increase in the cost of processing statutory planning relates to increased costs associated with consulting fees and legal fees associated with a number of high profile planning applications and matters called in by the State Government.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: There have been 10 decisions upheld at VCAT out of an overall 20 decisions  that were taken to appeal. This reflects the contentious and complex nature of some of the decisions.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: There has been a reduction in the number of missed bins which is attributed to a change in collection contractors. With the number of missed bins reducing each quarter, this trend is expected to continue next year.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: Following changes in recent years to bin collection, the service has returned to standardised operations, with implementation costs now normalised.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: An ongoing impact of changed bin collection frequencies continues to drive increased recyclables which is the desired outcome. This increase in volume contributes to a slight increase in cost of recycling, offset by the reduction in garbage.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: Council continues to sustain a high level of waste diverted from landfill and has met the target of 70%. There has been a reduction in co-mingled recycling relating to the introduction the container deposit scheme.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Council is committed to providing high quality services to the Bayside community in the most efficient way possible. Ongoing savings have continued to be found to keep expenses per head of municipal population low and measure is within the expected range.  The increase in expenses per head in 2023/24 is driven by a number of factors including the expansion of Council's fully funded Home Care Package Aged Care service, an increase in recurrent service costs funded from additional revenue, and increased depreciation due to Council's aggressive capital replacement program.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: The general rates and the municipal charge for 2023/24 increased by 3.5%, in accordance with the Fair Go Rates System. The waste charge increased 2.2%.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: Council's result is an indicator of a strong financial position.  This measure has remained at levels consistent with the prior year. Council will continue to utilise its cash reserves as part of its funding strategy to support its aggressive capital program. Liquidity levels will be maintained at sustainable levels into the future.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The decrease this year is due to higher carry forward capital works and statutory reserves resulting in less unrestricted cash.  Unrestricted cash is expected to decrease slowly over future years as Council funds it's aggressive capital program.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council continues to have no requirement for borrowing at this time.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Council continues to have no requirement for borrowing at this time.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: Own source revenue has continued to increase in 23/24 plus the result has been influenced by an increase in non current liabilities (employee provisions).

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: Council maintains a level of renewal and upgrade expenditure which is sufficient to ensure that its assets are renewed in accordance with condition assessment and service needs. The results have remained similar to the prior year.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: The underlying result will decrease slightly in future years as Bayside delivers an ambitious capital program funded from cash reserves, coupled with an increase in depreciation.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: There has been an increase in other sources of revenue, particularly user fees and interest income, and thus Council was slightly less reliant on rate revenue.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: The rate increase is in accordance with the rate capping framework.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: Council is committed to providing high quality services to the Bayside community in the most efficient way possible. The increase in expenses per head in 2023/24 is driven by a number of factors including a reduction in the population estimate, the expansion of Council's fully funded Home Care Package Aged Care service, an increase in recurrent service costs funded from additional revenue, and increased depreciation due to Council's aggressive capital replacement program.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: Bayside has outsourced all of its maintenance works and therefore holds very low levels of plant and equipment.  The value of Council's building assets is relatively low  given it is old and in need of an upgrade. Council has doubled the level of capital spend over the last five years to address this issue. This is reflected in the gradual increase in the ratio over time.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: The population density of Bayside is comparable to other metropolitan councils and reflects the relatively low density nature of bayside suburbs.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: Own source revenue had increased slightly in 23/24 as a result of growth in user fees, income from expanded aged care services and interest income from investments as interest rates continue to remain high.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation: Recurrent grants continue at a higher rate than previous years, including the expansion of Home Care packages resulting in $8.1million in recurrent grants from the federal government.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The rating indicates that overall, Bayside has a lower number of disadvantage when compared to most other local government areas in Victoria, and to metropolitan Melbourne. However, it is important to acknowledge that Bayside does have scattered pockets of neighbourhoods experiencing significant hardship and disadvantage, which is masked by the affluence across the municipality in general.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: Staff turnover has reduced slightly consistent with previous years, but includes some redundancies relating to changes to federal funding for aged care assessment, and some sectors such as construction that still experience labour market pressures and turnover. Concerted efforts to retain strong staff engagement keep the turnover rate lower than the metropolitan average for similar councils.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The service cost has increased slightly as it now includes capital purchases of library materials, which better reflects the true cost of providing a contemporary collection to the community. Other operational costs are consistent with previous years and remain well within the standard and are similar to other metropolitan councils.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: The result for this measure has increased due to increased inspections and water sampling conducted at the facility following a flood event.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: This measure has decreased due to lower than usual summer season temperatures resulting in lower casual entries to the facility. The adjacent free Splash Park is also thought to be influencing lower casual swim entry numbers.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: This measure has increased due to lower entry numbers in the prior year, plant and equipment maintenance costs increased due to breakdowns more than budget, staff oncosts increased due to wages growth, and the cost of materials and services increased greater than inflation forecasts used to set budgets at the start of the financial year.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: The cost of library services per population increased this year. This can be attributed to an increase in costs associated with the upgrade of library book return chutes at 5 libraries, as well as higher online subscription costs for electronic books, magazines and newspapers.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation: The number of inspections has increased from previous years in response to anticipated higher public health risks with waterborne diseases.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: Whilst attendances and memberships are below pre-COVID-19 pandemic levels, they are slowly continuing to increase compared to FY2022-23.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation: Financial performance is improving following the COVID-19 pandemic, successfully meeting the target.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: The time taken to action animal requests has stayed consistent compared to last year and is considered a timely and effective response time.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation: Animals reclaimed has decreased due to a change in Local Government Victoria's reporting requirements, which now includes animals surrendered by the public into the RSPCA. Surrendered animals is when a resident can no longer look after their animal anymore and are choosing to surrender it for various reasons, including financial, behavioural or changes in circumstance. Surrendered animals have a very low probability of being reclaimed and are more likely to be rehomed, hence impacting the overall reclaim result for Council.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation: Adoptions for cats has steadily increased by the RSPCA over the course of the year, which has improved the rehoming rate compared to last year. Cats continue to represent the majority of animals rehomed at approximately 85%, with dogs representing approximately 15%.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: The cost of animal management service has increased slightly from the previous year. This increase was due to the closure of animal registrations for residents who did not meet the April 2024 renewal deadline, leading to a higher write-off for funds that were unable to be collected in the final quarter of this financial year.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: Council maintains a high success rate of animal management prosecutions. Responding to public safety concerns regarding domestic animals is a high priority. The total number of animal prosecutions for the 2023-24 financial year was 15.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: The 2023-24 result has increased by 0.53 days from the 2022-23 result. This has had no impact on public health and Boroondara still prioritises responding to complaints about food premises.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: Council has consistently met its targets for food safety assessments, highlighting its commitment to protecting public health.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: The cost of food safety services has slightly increased from 2022-23, primarily due to salaries and food sampling, which is a statutory requirement.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: Close monitoring of this target has enabled Council to protect public health and meet target. The number of Class 1 and Class 2 premises that received an annual inspection in the 2023 calendar was 1,055.

Description: Food safety samples
Variation: This is a statutory target provided by the Department of Health (VIC) every calendar year. The result exceeded the target, effectively mitigating the risk of invalid samples and ensuring the desired outcome is achieved.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: The vast majority of Council decisions continue to be made in public. Some meetings do require a confidential session. In this year, these meetings related to contractual matters including receiving legal advice about those matters. Having those particular meetings, or parts of those meetings in public would waive Council’s client legal privilege.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation:
The overall satisfaction score for community consultation and engagement is 60 in 2024, up 1 point from 2023 (index score of 59). This is above the last 3 year average of 59.  This metric has historically been stable with no significant year on year shifts.  Boroondara continues to perform significantly above metro and state-wide averages (56 and 51 respectively).    
Further research in 2023 provided insights into factors affecting community perception of Council's performance in consultation and engagement, which resulted in the identifications of 14 quick wins which were implemented over the last year.  It is positive that consultation and engagement has recorded an increase this year and is scoring significantly higher than the metropolitan and statewide averages.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Councillor attendance at meetings this financial year was slightly lower than last year, but attendance remained high. The decrease was primarily due to councillor illness and other personal commitments. Councillors provided apologies in advance for meetings they were unable to attend.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The modest increase in costs reflects the increases in councillor allowances and increases in costs relating to the services associated with conducting Council meetings such as technical support and catering.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: The overall satisfaction score for council decisions is 60 in 2024, up 1 point from 2023 (index score of 59). This is slightly below the last 3 year average of 61. Last year, this metric went down by 2 points, in line with declining results seen across the state.  This year, we see a recovery of 1 point. Boroondara continues to perform significantly above metro and state-wide averages (57 and 50 respectively).  Perception in this area has historically been difficult to shift and Council has performed consistently on this measure between 59 and 63 for the past 10 years.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: The proportion of items less than 5 years of age in the collection has increased over the last 5 years, and the 2023-24 figure (66.92%) is higher than the 2022-23 all Council average of 62%. This result meets modern library standards.

Description: Loans per head of population
Variation: The total number of loans in 2023-24 is at the highest level since 2018-19 (pre- COVID-19).

Description: Library membership
Variation: Over 40% of library members have borrowed or reserved an item (physical or digital) in the last 36 months.

Description: Library visits per head of population
Variation: Library visitation has grown across 2023-24 and is at its highest level since pre-COVID-19. This total is an increase of 122,472 or 15.4% on the previous year.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: Infant enrolment is greater than birth notifications received due  to enrolments of infants born outside of Boroondara.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: The 2023-24 result remains within expected range, showing a slight increase compared to the 2022-23 actuals. This is due largely to increased casual utilisation related to sick leave and other unplanned leave, increased cost of staff safety initiatives (duress system), staff safety and additional staff training.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Annual participation is in line with expectations. The number of children that participated in the 2023-24 financial year was 4,066.50.  These results can vary as not all children are due for a key age and stage visit each year.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Annual participation of Aboriginal children in the MCH service remains high and has achieved annual target. The number of aboriginal children that participated in the 2023-24 financial year was 29.50.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Participation of infants for the 4 week key age and stage visits remains high and on target.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Council has had a decrease in road requests over the year. We attribute this to dryer conditions over the year resulting in less road maintenance requests.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: The City of Boroondara identified an increase in roads below intervention level through our 2021 road condition audit. Over the past 4 years, increased road funding has seen a steady decrease in roads requiring intervention.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: The current market rates for civil works relating to road reconstruction have been rising over the past 12 months and have also incurred a CPI contract increase impacting the quarterly results.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: The direct resealing cost per square metre of sealed local roads resealed has increased in the last 12 months. This has resulted in a slight rise in cost compared to previous years.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation:
The overall satisfaction score for sealed local roads is 70 in 2024, up 3 points from 2023 (index score of 67). Last year, this metric saw a significant decline of 4 points, in line with declining results across the state. The City of Boroondara identified an increase in roads requiring intervention in our 2021 road condition audit. As a result of the audit, we increased road funding, steadily decreasing the number of roads requiring intervention. 
While a score of 70 is still slightly below the last 3 year average of 71, this result shows a promising recovery attributed to the increased funding.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: The median time to decide on planning applications for FY2023-24 is 96 which is a decrease of 6 days from the previous financial year and a 5.88% improvement for this measure.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: 66.89% of Planning Permit and VicSmart applications were processed within the 60 and 10 day timeframes. This is an improvement of 8 percentage points compared to the previous financial year.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: For the 2023-24 financial year, 1,147 PPARS planning application and amendments were received which is 24 more than the amount reported in the previous financial year. There has been a reduction in costs compared with the previous year which has resulted in a lower cost of service in addition to a slightly greater number of applications being received which also reduces the cost of service per application.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: The result for decisions not set aside by VCAT is 48% compared with 44% in the previous financial year. It is noted that a high number of matters in quarters 1 and 2 were settled prior to a hearing, and those that did proceed to a hearing generally resulted in favourable outcomes. However, a lower number of decisions were favourable in quarters 3 and 4.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: There has been a significant improvement in the 2023-24 year end result compared to 2022-23. This positive change is due to improved results by the kerbside recycling collections contractor.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The overall cost associated with this measure is lower in 2023-24 compared to 2022-23. This is due to the removal of the costs associated with kerbside FOGO collection from this measure following an assessment of the kerbside garbage service.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: Council provides a weekly kerbside recycling service. The cost increases are due to the rise in labour and fuel costs increase throughout FY2023-24.  To counteract these increases, higher compaction rates have been implemented to minimise transportation costs.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The increase in this metric during 2021-22 was caused by the implementation of FOGO collection in May 2020. The reduction during 2023-24 is caused by the introduction of the Container Deposit Scheme in November 2023, diverting the higher density material away from the kerbside recycling stream.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Council continues to deliver services in accordance with its Long Term Financial Plan.  There has been a decrease in the overall expenditure primarily due to lower bad and doubtful debts and there was no loss on the disposal of property, infrastructure, plant and equipment and joint ventures (compared to 2022-23). This decrease is partially offset by an increase in materials and services and depreciation expense. Future forecasts are expected to remain steady.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: Council's budgeted rate increase in 2023-24 was capped at 3.50%.  The rate cap is set by the State Government's Fair Go Rates System (FGRS) and Council's forecast rate increases have been aligned to the forecast FGRS. The forecast rate increase for 2024-25 has been set at 2.75%.  Council is delivering services in accordance with its Long Term Financial Plan.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: The indicator was lower in 2020-21 due to the reduction of cash reserves, an increase in unearned income due to additional capital grants received and an increase in trust funds and deposits. During 2022-23, current assets decreased primarily due to the conditional grants unspent and a reduction in cash reserves. There was also a decrease in current liabilities associated with a reduction in unearned income and trade and other payables.  In 2023-24, current assets increased primarily due to Council holding $167.26 million in other financial assets at 30 June 2024. This increase was driven by higher interest rate returns, the sale of Serpells Land ($16 million) and the divestment of the Boroondara Tennis Centre ($30 million). Working capital remains well above the minimum sustainable level.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The unrestricted cash is lower primarily due to a reduction of cash reserves.  In 2020-21 and 2021-22, Council's own source revenue streams decreased as a result of the impacts of COVID-19. It started to recover in 2022-23.  For 2023-24, the unrestricted cash balance was lower due to Council investing $167.26 million of cash in term deposits with a maturity date greater than three months at 30 June 2024. During 2024-25, term deposits will be redeemed and transferred back to cash and cash equivalents. In the long term, unrestricted cash remains within a sustainable level.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: The low percentage in 2020-21 is due to a combination of higher rate revenue and lower principal repayments as Council continued to reduce existing debt. In 2012-13, Council continued with substantial investment in major building redevelopment works and borrowed $29 million.  The borrowings were at a fixed interest rate for 10 years and were due to be repaid in full in 2022-23. Council reviewed its existing loan portfolio in 2022-23 and refinanced the remainder of this loan for a further 10 years. Council also took out borrowings of $70 million in 2021-22 to fund significant infrastructure projects.  No new borrowings were taken out in 2023-24 and the decrease is due to lower principal repayments as Council continues to reduce existing debt. All existing borrowings are projected to be repaid by 2033.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: In 2012-13, Council continued with substantial investment in major building redevelopment works and borrowed $29 million. The borrowings were at a fixed interest rate for 10 years and were due to be repaid in full in 2022-23. Council reviewed its existing loan portfolio in 2022-23 and refinanced the remainder of this loan for a further 10 years. Council took out borrowings of $70 million in 2021-22 to fund significant infrastructure projects.  The decrease in 2023-24 is due to lower principal repayments as Council continues to reduce existing debt.  All existing borrowings are projected to be repaid by 2033.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: In 2020-21 and 2021-22 Council's own source revenue decreased due to the ongoing impacts of COVID-19 on Councils revenue streams, primarily in user fees and fines.  There was also an increase in non-current liabilities in 2021-22 as Council took out borrowings of $70 million to fund significant infrastructure projects.  In 2022-23 Council's own source revenue increased primarily in user fees and fines due to a decline in ongoing COVID-19 impacts on Council's operations. Council also reviewed its existing loan portfolio in 2022-23 and refinanced the remainder of its 2012-13 loan for a further 10 years.  In 2023-24 Council's own-source revenue increased primarily due to a net gain on disposal of property, infrastructure, plant and equipment and an increase in other income and user fees and charges. There was also a decrease in non-current liabilities due to Council's reduction on interest bearing loans and borrowings.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation:
Total expenses for 2023-24 include $1,085,000 in costs related to non-recurring projects, most of which were funded through grants. This represents a significant increase compared to the $238,000 incurred in the 2022-23 financial year. Additionally, $552,000 in capital expenditure, incurred over multiple financial years, was classified as operating expenses in 2023-24 due to not meeting capitalisation criteria. This too is included in the total expenses, compared to $772,000 in similar expenditure for 2022-23.

Excluding these non-recurring items, the result for 2023-24 is $4,039, compared to $3,827 for 2022-23 on the same basis. The approximately 5.2% increase in expenses per property assessment on a recurring basis reflects the inflationary pressures faced by the Council during 2023-24, resulting in expenses per property assessment exceeding both the target and last year's result on a recurring basis.

Furthermore, the majority of Queenscliffe's expenditure is non-discretionary and essential for managing the services expected of a local council. Due to the very small ratepayer base, this results in a higher expenditure per property assessment compared to other local councils

Variation: Rate revenue represents a high proportion of Queenscliffe’s revenue and spread across a very small ratepayer base.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: Brimbank City Council places a strong emphasis on working with applicants and objectors to achieve good outcomes in planning determinations. There has been a 26% improvement in the median number of days for processing applications in 2023-2024 compared to the previous year. This result is within the range set by Council.  Find out more about Brimbank’s Statutory Planning Service at https://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/building-and-planning/planning.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: Brimbank City Council is committed to providing an efficient and effective statutory planning service. Council has a very low number of VCAT appeals each year due to the work done to resolve issues when assessing applications.  In 2023/2024 only 14 planning applications were considered at VCAT, of which seven resulted in consent orders, one was remitted to Council for further consideration, two Council decisions were upheld, and four decisions were overturned. This result is within the range expected by Council.   Find out more about Brimbank’s Statutory Planning Service at https://www.brimbank.vic.gov.au/building-and-planning/planning.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards

The new data is showing that a greater number of roads have reached intervention levels than the previous data set was indicating. The roads that have reached intervention level have been included in the 2024-25 capital works renewal program. The increase in the number of roads that have reached intervention may be the result of the extremely wet weather that has been experienced over the last few years.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction

These were native vegetation removal which required an external specialist to be onsite when the work was carried out. Also, the nature of the road required roadside barriers (guard rails) to be installed on most of the length of the road. These are complications that have not been encountered on road reconstructions carried out in previous years and resulted in a large increase in the cost per square metre of reconstruction.

Variation: The cost of inputs related to road resealing has increased. This has resulted in a higher per meter cost than previous years.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: The result of Council not receiving the 2024/25 financial assistance grant funding of $13.46 million in advance before 30 June 2024 (as had been the practice in previous financial years). Had Council received the funding in advance, the percentage would have been 404.60%. This is still below the 454.75% for 2022/23 actual, however, Council did receive grant funding for the October 2022 flood as well as not expend the planned capital works program (due to the flood), which contributed to the 454.75% for the 2022/23 financial year.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: When compared to the previous years, overall reduction in cash held by Council due to expending 2022/23 capital works carryover of over $12 million, as well as Council not receiving the 2024/25 financial assistance grant funding of $13.46 million in advance before 30 June 2024 (as had been the practice in previous financial years).

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council continues to pay down loans each financial year, resulting in this percentage decreasing towards 0% (forecast to occur in the 2026/27 financial year).

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Council will continue to pay down current borrowing levels and will be fully debt free by end of 2026/27 financial year. Council currently has no future borrowing forecasted in the budget.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: Reduction is the result of Council paying down loans by $2.66 million for the 2023/24 financial year, when compared to the 2022/23 financial year.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: Council's 2022/23 percentage was impacted by the October 2022 flood, which resulted in planned renewal and upgrade capital works not being started or started late (and not completed) in the 2022/23 financial year. These projects, for a total over $12 million,  were rolled into 2023/24 financial year and completed. Essentially, a timing variance.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: The result of Council not receiving the 2024/25 financial assistance grant funding of $13.46 million in advance before 30 June 2024 (as had been the practice in previous financial years), as well as not budgeting for the net loss of disposal of property, infrastructure, plant and equipment of $7.35 million. Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation:
1. The increase in the ratio is primarily due to the rise in the cash balance, excluding term deposits.

2. As of 30 June 2024, $115 million is held in term deposits (compared to $325 million on 30 June 2023). These deposits are classified as other financial assets, not cash, because their terms exceed 90 days.

3. If term deposits were included, the unrestricted cash balance would be $100.13 million as of 30 June 2024 (compared to $173.32 million as of 30 June 2023).

4. The revised ratio would be 106.31% as of 30 June 2024 (down from 177.41% as of 30 June 2023).

5. The ratio decreases by 40% due to substantial capital works expenditure exceeding $149 million this year, significantly reducing the total cash and term deposits at the 30 June 2024 closing balance compared to 2023.

6. Over the next four years, this ratio is expected to decline due to a substantial capital works program, which is projected to notably reduce the cash balance.
