Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: The SEIFA relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage score is measured every five years. The score summarises a range of information about the economic and social conditions of people and households within the City. It indicates that there was an increase in disadvantage when compared to other local government areas in the most recent results. There are several pockets of disadvantage and vulnerable members of our community are experiencing mental health issues, substance abuse problems, childhood developmental difficulties, insecure housing and employment. Building a safer and active community with strong social connections is key to supporting the community we serve.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: 2023/24 has again seen a significant reduction in turnover returning to pre-pandemic levels. Work continues with hiring teams to improve hiring standards to ensure the best candidates and job alignment for each vacant role. As reflected across both the private and broader public sector, some professions within the organisation continue to see challenges in the labour market. City of Port Phillip continues to strive to be an employer of choice and will continue to focus on both our attraction and retention strategies.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Council is delivering quality services in accordance with its long-term plan. The increase in this indicator compared to 2022-23 is primarily driven by increased employee costs (including mandated superannuation increases, Enterprise Agreement increases and increases in annual leave and long service leave provisions, as well as the redundancy cost associated with the exit out of the Commonwealth Home Support Program); and inflationary impacts on materials and services. In addition, depreciation and amortisation costs have increased from the capital and Digital Transformation programs, as well as the impairment of intangible assets. This has resulted in an increase in annual operating expenditure from $205.04 million in 2022-23 to $219.52 million in 2023-24.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: Council continues to have one of the lowest average residential rates and charges across metropolitan Melbourne. Council’s actual rate increase was capped at 3.5 per cent for 2023-24 together with an increased number of property assessments.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: The Council can comfortably meet all short-term financial commitments. The lower working capital ratio in 2023-24 compared to prior years is due to $41.00 million of borrowings that are classified as current and will be re-financed in 2024-25. Working capital is expected to range between 95-119% over the next four financial years, lower than historical levels due to the lost revenue over the pandemic and the continued investment in our capital program.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The prior year results do not include Council's holdings of Term Deposits with maturity over 90 days (which are classed as other Financial Assets). These Term Deposits total $31.0 million in 2023-24. When included in the measure for 2023-24 the result is 27.9 per cent (2022-23, 82.2 per cent). Forecasts for 2024-25 onwards assume that all term deposits as having original maturities of less than 90 days and are therefore included in unrestricted cash.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: During the financial year, Council borrowed $14.50 million to fund the capital works program. This was approved within the 2023-24 Budget adoption and sits within the expected range. It is consistent with Council's long term financial plan and pay-back strategy.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Council made principal loan repayments of $2.37 million in 2023-24. New loans and associated repayments are forecast in the next 4 years to assist in funding major community infrastructure. This is consistent with Council's long term financial plan.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: The drop in the 2023-24 actual is due to $41.00 million of loans in current liabilities, which will be re-borrowed in 2024-25. The trend reflects Council's medium-term borrowings strategy to fund the capital works program over the next four years. Additional loan borrowings of $7.0 million for 2024-25, $5.8 million for 2025-26, $10.0 million for 2026-27 and $8.0 million for 2027-28 are forecast to assist in funding community infrastructure.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: This metric is above the expected range, and illustrates Council’s focus on ensuring a sustainable level of funding is provided for the renewal of community infrastructure. The metric is below target assumptions due to higher depreciation driven by revaluations and capitalisation at the end of the previous year. Council has a robust capital program that ensures appropriate levels of renewals and upgrades are maintained. Council has allocated sufficient funding to the capital works program to meet its renewal and upgrade requirements in future years.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: From 2021-22 through to 2023-24, the adjusted underlying result is lower than previous years, mainly due to an increase in annual operating expenditure. This is due to the application of IAS 38 Intangible Assets – Configuration or Customisation Costs in a Cloud Computing Arrangement which has impacted Council's results. In 2023-24 this resulted in $5.40 million of Digital Transformation costs expensed and a net loss of $6.10 million in impairing the WIP balance of the Digital Transformation Program for future expected expenses. Results have also been impacted by the write-off of property and infrastructure assets during the year of $4.43 million. In addition, employee costs, inflationary impacts and depreciation have also added to higher expenditure, refer to ‘expenses per property assessment’ for further details.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: The 2023-24 result is consistent with the 2022-23 result. Rate revenue will continue to be a key source of funding for the delivery of high quality services and infrastructure to the community.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation: This result illustrates the relatively low rating burden for the Stonnington community, and Council continues to have one of the lowest average residential rates and charges across metropolitan Melbourne.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation:
Council received a total of 18 food complaints in 2023 which is eight more than 2022. 
This demonstrates that community members are aware they can report concerns about the safety or handling of food that is sold within Wellington Shire via Council's Customer Action Request system. 
To minimise any further risk to the community, Council is committed to responding to food safety complaints as a priority. 
This is demonstrated by the 2023 results once again showing all food safety related complaints were responded to within 1 day.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation:
For the year ending 31 December 2023, 38 premises required a food safety assessment with 36 food safety assessments being undertaken. The high inspection rate demonstrates that Council has prioritised the conduct of these inspections. 
The two premises not undertaken were due to scheduling difficulties with business operators. 
Numbers required for assessments continues to vary each year due to premises closures, new registrations and change in business activities altering the Food Act requirements.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: Direct cost of Council's food safety program per all registered and notifiable food premises is $386.45. The cost of delivering food safety service has remained reasonably steady during the last couple of years.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: For the 2023 calendar year, there were 18 non-compliance notifications. All 18 food premises received one or more follow up inspections to ensure compliance with the Food Act 1984.

Description: Food safety samples
Variation:
For the year ending 31 December 2023, Wellington Shire Council were required under the Food Act 1984 to obtain 72 food samples. 
9 samples must come from a Class 1 premises and 63 from a Class 2 premises. 
78 food samples were obtained by Council officers – 12 samples from Class 1 premises and 66 samples from Class 2 premises. Council exceeded the 100% sampling requirement.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation:

All council meetings open to the public are broadcast live via Council's website and made available via an online video archive. 
Council actively strives to limit decisions made in closed session to ensure transparency and accountability to the community in its decision making.

Wellington Shire was also impacted by unprecedented Bushfires and Floods in quick succession which saw many residents seeking refuge in our library facilities.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation:
The number of customer action requests for local sealed roads has decreased by approximately 20% when compared to the previous 2022/23 financial year. 
Whilst Wellington Shire did experience storm and heavy rain events, there were prolonged periods of dry weather which has likely contributed towards the decrease in requests. 
Wellington Shire has also been focusing on works to rehabilitate roads in poor condition or impacted by emergencies through both our capital and maintenance programs.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation:
The percentage of roads below the set intervention level is 99.23%, which is an improvement of the previous year’s results of 97.84%. 
Over the last few years, Wellington Shire’s road network has been impacted by a number of emergency storm and rain events causing a number of land slips, as well as damage across our low lying road network. 
Wellington Shire focused on emergency repair works and the renewal of its poor condition assets as part of its 2023/24 capital works program, which has resulted in the improved figure. 
This investment will continue in 2024/25 and will begin to include roads which are approaching our set condition level.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation:
The cost of sealed local road reconstruction has slightly decreased compared to the previous financial year. 
Council’s 2023/24 capital works program did contain some reconstruction jobs in Urban areas, but it primarily focused on larger rural road reconstruction and widening works using spray seal rather than asphalt. 
Given the scale of the projects, this is considered a likely reason why the overall cost decreased.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: In 2023/24, the unit rate for Wellington Shire Council’s road resealing program has slightly increased compared to the 2022/23 financial year. The cost of bitumen has remained steady over the last 12 months for our area, meaning that our reseal rates have been stable.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation:
Results from the 2024 Community Satisfaction Survey shows no change from the previous year in resident’s satisfaction rating for Wellington Shire’s sealed local roads compared to the 2023 Community Satisfaction Survey.
Wellington Shire has continued to be impacted by ongoing storm and rain events with high intensity rainfalls and flooding impacting the majority of the Shire.
Some planned maintenance works were delayed so our maintenance teams could focus on the immediate clean up and repair activities following these events.
Wellington Shire’s capital program has focussed on the reconstruction and major maintenance of many of our poor condition sealed roads and the results can be seen in the Sealed Road Condition percentage figures. 
This focus on major renewal works will continue into the 2024/25 financial year. 
Wellington Shire Council is responsible for a road network of 3,112km, where 1,549km are sealed and 1,563km are unsealed.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames

Council has achieved good results with 90.1% of standard applications and 91.89% of VicSmart applications being decided within specified time frames, compared to the State result of 62.98% and 79.9% respectively.

626 bins were reported as missed during 2023/24. 
The transition to a new collection contractor in September has resulted in a decrease in bins missed.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation:
Wellington Shire's kerbside collection includes the weekly garbage waste collection service of over 20,600 bins across the municipality. Additional services for residents in Wellington Shire, not incorporated in this cost, include an annual hard waste collection service, and our annual greenwaste program and a fortnightly recycling bin collection service. 
The procurement of a new collection and transport contractor contributed to the reduction in costs of delivery of the kerbside waste service.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: There has been approximately 10% reduction in the amount of kerbside recycling compared to the 2022/2023 financial year likely due to the impact of the Container Deposit Scheme (CDS) introduced in November 2023.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation:
More than 3,300 tonnes of recyclable material were diverted from landfill in 2023/24. 
This does not include food organics and garden organics as there is no current service provided, nor does it include the diverted material through the introduction of the Container Deposit Scheme (CDS). 
With an average of 160kg of recyclables per kerbside collection household in Wellington Shire, a reduction of 18kg per household has been achieved when compared to 22/23 figures this could be a direct result of the introduction of the CDS. 
Council is working towards the future implementation of a Food and Garden Organics collection which will divert additional waste from landfill.

Variation: There has been an increase in the number of animals rehomed this financial year. This demonstrates Council's successful partnership with the Pound Contract Provider who have actively promoted the rehoming of unclaimed animals from our municipality.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: Council continues to deliver community education, effective pound management through Animal Aid, and address compliance matters. We also offer extended hours and conduct proactive patrols outside of normal business hours. Our commitment remains steadfast in providing a high-quality and cost-effective animal management service for our community.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: This year, Council maintained a 100% successful prosecution rate for all animal-related matters, prosecuting nine cases in total. Council pursues prosecution for cases that cannot be resolved with the relevant parties outside of court.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: This is a calendar year result, and as such the final result for the 2023/2024 year. Council’s target for responding to food complaints is 2.5 days, and with complaints typically responded to by the next business day, the result is well within the target.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: This is a calendar year result, and as such the final result for the 2023/2024 year. As of 31 December 2023 there were 910 assessments on registered Class 1 and 2 Food premises, including mobile food premises. The total number of registrations fluctuate during the course of the year depending on the number of new and closed registrations. All Class 1 and 2 registered Food premises requiring an assessment had an Annual Food Safety Assessment or a Final Inspection in the case of a new premises

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: As of 31 December 2023 there were 1,398 registered/notified food premises, including temporary/mobile food premises. The total number of registrations fluctuate during the course of the year depending on the number of new and closed registrations. The decrease in cost this year is due to a higher number of food premises registered within the municipality compared to previous years.  The direct cost is based on 75% on operating expenditure for the Environmental Health Operations Program.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: This is a calendar year result, and as such the final result for the 2023/2024 year. There were 56 assessments/inspections resulting in Major/Critical non-compliance this year, and all were followed up during the reporting period.

Description: Food safety samples
Variation: This is a new calendar year measure and as such, the final result for the 2023/2024 year. The number of food samples Council is required to complete is determined by the State Government and published in the Victorian Government Gazette. The total gazetted number of food samples for the 2023 calendar year is 209. Council exceeded the target with 254 food samples obtained, 111 of these obtained from July to December 2023.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: A total of ten (10) items were deemed confidential in accordance with s3(1) of the Local Government Act 2020 over the 2023/2024 financial year. Reasons for confidentiality included Council information that would be prejudicial, personal information, and private commercial information. The overall result of 5.2% is below the metropolitan and state averages and is lower than the results of previous years, consistent with Council’s ongoing commitment to public transparency.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: The 2024 community satisfaction result for Council's consultation and engagement has increased since the 2022/23 year. The increase demonstrates Council's commitment to improve community engagement activities and further support the needs of the community.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: Council meeting attendance overall for FY 2023/2024 was 97.3%. The variation from earlier years' figures is due to a change in how attendance is measured, with apologies no longer being recorded as attendances. This result remains below metropolitan and state averages.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The cost of elected representation has increased slightly this financial year, but has done so at well below the rate of inflation, and remains below metropolitan and state averages.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: This result is from the 2024 community satisfaction survey and shows an increase in the satisfaction for Council's decision making. This increase demonstrates the ongoing commitment by Councillors to make improved and transparent decisions that achieve the best outcomes for the community.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: This result is a slight improvement on the previous year. Whitehorse Manningham Libraries continues to work through a systematic assessment and withdrawal process of older material.

Description: Loans per head of population
Variation: This is a new measure for 2023/24 and the result for this financial year is within the expected range determined by Local Government Victoria. This result demonstrates a high number of library loans for the Whitehorse population.

Description: Library membership
Variation: This is a new measure for 2023/24 and the result for this financial year is within the expected range determined by Local Government Victoria. This result demonstrates a high number of library memberships for the Whitehorse population.

Description: Library visits per head of population
Variation: This is a new measure for 2023/24 and the result for this financial year is within the expected range determined by Local Government Victoria. Whitehorse Manningham libraries continues to maintain strong library visits in Whitehorse.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: Council continues to see high infant enrolments in the Maternal and Child Health Service, despite the decline in overall birth notifications throughout the municipality. The percentage is above 100% due to babies born outside the municipality moving into Whitehorse prior to their enrolment in the service.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: Council continues to provide a cost effective Maternal and Child Health service for the Whitehorse community, with education and support services for all families with children from birth to school age. Council's annual result in line with previous reporting periods and the service budget.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Council continues to see a relatively stable participation rate in the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Service; with a range of active promotional activities being utilised to support client engagement.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: The Whitehorse municipality has a small number of Indigenous Australian children registered as part of the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) service. The participation rate remains reasonably high as Council maintains the responsiveness of the Enhanced MCH Program.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Council continues to see a stable participation rate in the 4 week Key Age and Stage visits as part of the Maternal and Child Health service, aligned with the high infant enrolment rates for the service.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: The number of sealed local road requests have decreased compared to 2022/23. In 2022/23 there were several high intensity rainfall event  that impacted the condition of roads. There is an ongoing impact that development works are having in 2023/24 with heavy vehicle traffic impacting the condition of local roads.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: Council has historically achieved a good result for this indicator, and this has continued in the 2023/24 financial year. The road condition audit completed in 2021/22 contributed to the development of a specified program of works to maintain our road condition standards. *This result, and the result for 2021/22 and 2022/23, is therefore based on the Road Management Audit data from 2021/22. A new road condition audit is scheduled for 2024/25, which will provide updated condition data.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: This amount is inclusive of contingencies, provisional items and project management fees. The projects for the year included road rehabilitation of the following existing sealed roads at Monash St, Box Hill South, Wallace Road, Burwood, Marlborough Street, Mont Albert and Troy Court, Forest Hill and the reconstruction of the brick laneway (known as Laneway 203) in Mitcham.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: The cost of scheduled resealing for local roads has remained consistent this year, aligning with previous years and staying within the budget.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: The result of the 2024 Community Satisfaction Survey for Road condition remains consistent with previous years. Council continues to work through our road maintenance program to ensure the condition of the sealed local roads are improving throughout the municipality.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: This year, Council's results remains significantly lower than the average Metropolitan time to determine planning applications. This result demonstrates Council's ongoing commitment in improving the planning application process for the Whitehorse community.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: This result has consistently increased over the last few reporting periods. This is a result of internal improvements to decision making and application processes, primarily relating to the VicSmart decision timeframes.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The cost of the statutory planning service has remained similar to the previous financial year.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation: This result continues to increase and be consistent with the trend across many previous years. This demonstrates consistent policy application by officers which has been further supported by the decisions at VCAT.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: There has been a slight increase in missed bins since the last reporting period. However, missed bins are still fewer compared to the same time last year. Our resident and driver education is ongoing.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: Since the introduction of the FOGO service, the volume of garbage collected remains consistent with the previous reporting period and same time last year. The increase in cost is a result of increasing disposal costs.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: The cost of the kerbside recycling service has continued to rise due to a substantial increase in processing costs.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: The proportion of waste diverted from landfill remains consistent with previous reporting period. The introduction of the State Government Container Deposit Scheme has resulted in a reduction of recycling tonnes collected which has impacted the diversion rate.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: This result demonstrates Council's continual ability to deliver services to the community within a responsible budget.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: This result confirms Whitehorse City Council's low average rates per assessment, which is among the lowest across Metropolitan Melbourne. The decrease in average rates per assessment in 2023/24 reflects the introduction and separation of the waste service charge which is excluded from general rates and this indicator.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation:
Working capital is higher in 2023/24 due to higher cash holdings at balance date and higher ‘other assets” mainly from accrued income relating to the divestment of Sinnott Street reserve, Burwood ($9.53m).  Current liabilities are lower in 2023/24 due to timing of trade and other payables and higher liabilities in 2022/23 relating to major capital projects and the provision of once-off employee entitlements due to Council’s decision not to renew its contracts to provide Whitehorse Home and Community Service beyond 30 June 2023.  

The 2023/24 result is well above the minimum sustainable level and is forecast to remain so, with decreases attributed mainly to the funding of major capital works and initiatives in future years.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: This indicator shows cash and cash equivalents and financial assets that are not available for use other than for the purpose for which it is restricted in accordance with accounting standards.  The unrestricted cash indicator for 2023/24 is due to cash held to fund carry forward capital works from 2023/24, conditional grants unspent and statutory reserves. Also contributing to the 2023/24 result were high levels of funding held in investments with a term of greater than 90 days maturity in order to maximise interest income at the end of 30 June 2024.  A total of $170 million in term deposit investments are classified as "other financial assets" not cash. If these term deposits were classified as cash the indicator result would be 188.22% (154.32% in 2022/23).

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council currently have no loans and borrowings

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: Council currently have no loans and borrowings

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation:
The 2023/24 result reflects an overall increase in own source revenue mainly due to proceeds from the divestment of the Sinnott Street reserve, Burwood ($9.53m) to the State Government for construction of the Suburban Rail Loop, higher interest on investments ($3.94m) and higher statutory fees and charges ($2.62m).  

Non-current liabilities have decreased in 2023/24, primarily relating to a decrease in lease liabilities as lease payments have been made during the course of the year.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation:
The indicator is lower than projected due to a combination of higher than budgeted depreciation, impacted by road and pathway revaluation increments and higher than budgeted depreciation on the recently capitalised The Round and Morack Public Golf major redevelopment projects during the year.  Also contributing to the result is lower than budgeted renewal and upgrade capital expenditure resulting from projects not progressing as rapidly as planned due to grant funding agreement delays, including the Box Hill City Oval, Mirrabooka and Forest Hill Reserve pavilions, and the Elgar Park North East oval synthetic surface project.

The forecast result is expected to return to above the desired level of 100% and remain strong, and reflects Council's continued commitment to renew its existing community infrastructure.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation:
The adjusted underlying result has improved returning a positive result for 2023/24.  Contributing to this result include higher revenue from the proceeds on the disposal of Sinnott Street reserve ($9.53m) to the State Government for construction of the Suburban Rail Loop, higher interest on investments ($3.94m) and higher statutory fees and charges ($2.62m).  This has been partly offset by a reduction in recurrent operating grant income, due to the entire 2023/24 funding allocation being paid early and recognised in 2022/23 ($5.78m) and reductions in Home & Community Services funding ($9.60m) and expenditure due to Council's decision not to renew its contracts to provide Whitehorse Home & Community Services beyond 30 June 2023.    

The prior year result of -4.06% included the impact of several once-off items including the entire funding allocation for 2023/24 being paid early and recognised in 2022/23, offset by once-off employee expenditure associated with the discontinuation of delivering Home & Community Services. 

The adjusted underlying result over the next four years reflects Council's investment in transformation initiatives that support the delivery of actions in the Council Plan.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: The indicator assesses whether council can generate revenue from a range of sources to fund services and activities. A lower proportion of rates to underlying revenue suggests greater stability.  For 2023/24, there is a slightly higher proportion of rates to underlying revenue compared to 2022/23, mainly due to the transfer of supplementary bin services (previously a fee for service under user fees) into rates and charges as a result of the introduction of Council's waste service charge.

Description: Rates compared to property values
Variation:
This result reflects the extent of reliance on rate revenues to fund all of Council's ongoing services.  A low or decreasing level of rates suggests an improvement in the rating burden.  Council's result remains low, with the forecast in alignment with historical performance. 

Overall property values in 2023/24 decreased by 2.52% compared to 2022/23, combined with the rate cap of 3.5% and inclusion of supplementary bin services (previously user fees) now included under rates and charges due to introduction of the waste service charge.

Description: Expenses per head of municipal population
Variation: This result demonstrates Council's ability to maintain a low cost base per head of population.  The 2023/24 result reflects a reduction in overall expenditure, due mainly to the inclusion in the prior year result of once-off employee related costs related to the discontinuation of services associated with Whitehorse Home and Community Services.

Description: Infrastructure per head of municipal population
Variation: The 2023/24 result is consistent with the prior year and reflects Council's continual commitment to invest in high-quality infrastructure.

Description: Population density per length of road
Variation: This result demonstrates the City of Whitehorse's population using an established road network, which is well maintained but not growing in length.  The increase in 2023/24 compared to 2022/23 is due to an increase in population growth of 3.51%.

Description: Own-source revenue per head of municipal population
Variation: The 2023/24 result is a combination of an overall increase in own source revenue mainly due to proceeds from the divestment of the Sinnott Street reserve, Burwood ($9.53m) to the State Government for construction of the Suburban Rail Loop, higher interest on investments ($3.94m) and higher statutory fees and charges ($2.62m) partly offset by a 3.51% increase in population growth in 2023/24.

Description: Recurrent grants per head of municipal population
Variation:
The 2023/24 result did not include the full year allocation of the Victorian Local Government Grants Commission 2023/24, with the entire amount being brought forward and included in 2022/23 year income. In addition, there has also been a reduction in recurrent grant income associated with Whitehorse Home & Community Services, due to Council's decision not to renew the service contracts.  

Population growth within the municipality has increased by 3.51% for 2023/24.

Description: Relative Socio-Economic Disadvantage
Variation: This result indicates that Whitehorse continues to be a municipality with a relatively low socio-economic disadvantage.

Description: Percentage of staff turnover
Variation: The higher staff turnover rate for 2023/24 is primarily due to Home and Community Services staff departures in the first quarter of 2023/24 as Council transitioned out of the Commonwealth Home Support Programme which concluded at 30 June 2023.  If this transition hadn’t taken place, the turnover rate would have been significantly lower, at 13%.

Description: Health inspections of aquatic facilities
Variation:
During 2023-24, Council inspected all three aquatic facilities a total of eight times (three inspections per indoor pool and two inspections for the outdoor pool which is only open during the summer months). 
All inspections and analysis returned compliant result, and it was confirmed that venue operators tested the water quality every four hours.
All privately owned pools/spas accessible to the public were tested according to the requirements of the Public Health & Wellbeing Act.

Description: Utilisation of aquatic facilities
Variation: Pool visits continue to increase year-on-year with visitations exceeding pre-pandemic levels. A number of successful programs have resulted in growth in participation, with both Mill Park Leisure (MPL) and Whittlesea Swim Centre (WSC) increasing by more than 14% and Thomastown Aquatic and Recreation Centre (TRAC) by 10%. Slightly warmer weather than last year also had a positive impact, allowing WSC to extend opening hours for 23 days.

Description: Cost of aquatic facilities
Variation:
Council aquatic facilities performed well financially, with a 56% increase on performance for Mill Park Leisure (MPL), resulting in a profit to Council, and a 70% improvement for Thomastown Recreation and Aquatic Centre (TRAC). 
Membership numbers improved significantly over the period due to a successful membership campaign, upgraded health club equipment at Thomastown Recreation and Aquatic Centre, and reduced visitor concerns regarding the pandemic.

Description: Time taken to action animal management requests
Variation: Council responded to 75% of the 2600 animal-related requests on the same working day during the financial year, the remaining requests were received after hours and were attended to on the next working day.

Description: Animals reclaimed
Variation:
Of the 2,617 animals collected during 2023-24, 34% were reclaimed. This result is largely driven by unclaimed cats, which is a trend seen across the sector. 
Council continues to provide responsible pet ownership education with a particular focus on feral cats which account for a high proportion of unclaimed animals.
Definition of feral animal: currently our systems are structured to record data in accordance with the data reporting framework established for the Code of Practice for the Management of Dogs and Cats in Shelters and Pounds.

Description: Animals rehomed
Variation:
Of the 2,617 animals collected during 2023-24, 43% have been rehomed. This is a favourable outcome given the overabundance of cats in the area, and the cost of living pressures affecting pet owners. 
A further 45% of animals collected were transferred out to foster care networks for rehoming.

Description: Cost of animal management service per population
Variation: Service improvements in animal management have reduced costs compared to last year. Council continues to refine the delivery model for valued services such as reuniting lost pets with their owners, pet adoptions, animal-related investigations, an after-hours emergency service and auditing animal-related businesses to ensure welfare standards are upheld. Please note the service cost amount also includes a proportion of the management and overhead costs as outlined in the wat djerring Animal Facility shared services contract.

Description: Animal management prosecutions
Variation: During the 2023-24 financial year, Council successfully prosecuted seven animal management matters.

Description: Time taken to action food complaints
Variation: In 2023, Council received 125 food complaints. Council provided a first response to all complaints within one working day.

Description: Food safety assessments
Variation: In 2023, Council assessed 99.9% of all Class 1 and Class 2 food premises.  Unfortunately, one food premises could not be assessed as it was closed to the public at the end of 2023.  It will be assessed when it reopens in late 2024.

Description: Cost of food safety service
Variation: There are more than 1600 registered food premises in the City of Whittlesea, with this number remaining consistent over the last two reporting periods. As a regulator, Council conducts routine food sampling to rest food safety and responds to food-related complaints. The increase in the cost of service this financial year can be attributed to increases to the cost of laboratory services and costs to recruit to vacant roles.

Description: Critical and major non-compliance outcome notifications
Variation: In 2023, Council conducted 115 follow up inspections which were identified as having either a critical or major non-compliance. Council has achieved a 100% result.

Description: Food safety samples
Variation: In 2023, Council obtained a total of 237 routine food samples which complied with the mandated sample number set by the State. Council achieved a service target of 100%.

Description: Council decisions made at meetings closed to the public
Variation: Decisions made at closed meetings slightly increased due to contractual matters containing commercial in confidence information, and CEO employment matters. The result is also reflective of Administrators not putting forward their own motions for consideration therefore the overall number of agenda items put to Council for decision making is lower than other similar size Councils.

Description: Satisfaction with community consultation and engagement
Variation: Council continues to authentically engage with our local community, to ensure their voices are considered in decision-making. In 2023-24 we consulted on 44 projects, held 159 community-based pop-ups, and received over 9000 contributions from community. Council endorsed an update to the Community Engagement Policy in December 2023 to support continuous improvement of the engagement function.

Description: Councillor attendance at council meetings
Variation: The Panel of Administrators attendance at Council meetings continues to be exceptional.

Description: Cost of elected representation
Variation: The Panel of Administrators allowances is set by the State Government and takes into consideration the Victorian Independent Remuneration Tribunal who set the allowances and any annual adjustments.

Description: Satisfaction with council decisions
Variation: Council has continued to consider the needs of the community when making decisions at Council meetings.

Description: Recently purchased library collection
Variation: The total number of collection items reflects the impact of the new Mernda Branch. This has resulted in maintaining the percentage rate of the collection less than 5 years old for this year. However, the rising costs of collection and associated costs will continue to impact on this KPI in subsequent years.

Description: Cost of library service per population
Variation: Direct costs are apportioned to member Councils by the Library Agreements. Costs have increased due to the general increase of operational costs across the library. The Yarra Plenty Regional Library service is a shared service for the local government areas of Banyule, Nillumbik and Whittlesea.

Description: Loans per head of population
Variation: With an increased collection size and new library access points such as the addition of the new Mernda Library, Council is seeing an increase in the total number of loans.

Description: Library membership
Variation: The opening of the new Mernda Library has seen a steady increase in library memberships with 2,289 new members. The addition of Click and Collect library hubs and mini branches within new and growing communities is also helping to address access to library services in these areas.

Description: Library visits per head of population
Variation: This year with the opening of the new Mernda Library, we have seen large attendance numbers for this branch. With both Lalor and Thomastown being closed for renovations during the year, we have still had an increase of 9.36% compared to the same period last year with October 2023 being our busiest month.

Description: Infant enrolments in the MCH service
Variation: This result exceeds 100% due to babies who are born outside the municipality moving to the City of Whittlesea shortly after birth.

Description: Cost of the MCH service
Variation: Council continue to experience workforce shortages in nursing, which has resulted in vacancies and increased costs (including new EBA), our costs continue to be lower than the Interface and metro averages. Council continues to recruit MCH nurses to join our team and work with our community.

Description: Participation in the MCH service
Variation: Council result has improved year-on-year, which reflects the service’s recovery from the pandemic. However, Council continues to be impacted by workforce shortages in the MCH sector.

Description: Participation in the MCH service by Aboriginal children
Variation: Council has improved engagement with our Aboriginal community through our Deadly Boorais, Deadly Families program.

Description: Participation in 4-week Key Age and Stage visit
Variation: Council has experienced an increase in the important Key Age and Stage visits, demonstrating a high level of engagement with our community.

Description: Sealed local road requests
Variation: Council has experienced a significantly higher number of sealed road requests over the entire year as these local roads are now generally used as alternative routes because of the large influx of developments and VicRoads works. Along with this addition to the road use, Council has noted more flooding events over the Spring and Summer seasons.

Description: Sealed local roads maintained to condition standards
Variation: This year has seen significant improvement in the number of sealed local roads maintained to condition standards. This reflects a combination of completed road asset renewals and the addition of new roads to Council's Asset Register. Late in the year a condition audit was commissioned for the sealed local road network, confirming that a very high proportion of roads are below intervention level.

Description: Cost of sealed local road reconstruction
Variation: Council road reconstruction costs are relatively stabilised when compared to previous years despite the escalating costs for labour and materials in this sector. This is due to the application of more efficient and effective reconstruction techniques based on local engineering knowledge and technical expertise. Projects are also programmed to maximise the efficient use of resources to capitalise on economies of scale as well as reducing the impact to residents and other stakeholders.

Description: Cost of sealed local road resealing
Variation: Council road resealing costs are relatively stabilised when compared with previous years. This is due to the application of more efficient and effective resealing techniques based on local engineering knowledge and technical expertise. Projects are also programmed to maximise the efficient use of resources to capitalise on economies of scale as well as reducing the impact to residents and other stakeholders.

Description: Satisfaction with sealed local roads
Variation: Council continues to work through our road construction and maintenance programming to provide a satisfactory road user experience. Several arterial road projects – while beneficial in the long term – have impacted on the local road user experience this year, particularly in Council’s northern areas. Council acknowledges that community sentiment about road condition is likely negatively impacted by the state of arterial roads, and to this end Council continues to work closely with State Government to influence arterial road outcomes, to ensure our road network accommodates the rapid growth of our municipality.

Description: Time taken to decide planning applications
Variation: Council’s median processing days to determine an application is 57 days for this financial year. This is well below the median for Growth Area Councils of 118 days.

Description: Planning applications decided within required time frames
Variation: Council delivered 67% of our decisions within the required time frame for the financial year.  While this is a slight reduction from previous years due to the complexity and quality of applications, Council continues to issue permits effectively and efficiently, benchmarking well against other interface Councils.

Description: Cost of statutory planning service
Variation: The operational cost of the planning service has increased slightly compared to 2023-24, while the number of applications has reduced, noting that the complexity of applications has increased. Please also note that the number of applications contributing to the data does not include post permit applications, ministerial approval referrals and officer time spent on DTP’s Planning Facilitation Programs, which has increased significantly this year.

Description: Council planning decisions upheld at VCAT
Variation:
Council aims to achieve mutually beneficial outcomes with all parties to avoid tribunal hearings in the first instance. Twelve of 18 decisions (67%) were either upheld by the Tribunal or resolved via negotiation with the applicant prior to hearing. We have a great deal of success with this approach, which indicates that the cases that do go to Tribunal are genuine cases that need independent adjudication.  It must be noted that applications lodged at VCAT often are very different to those originally lodged with Council. 
This result is variable each year and depends on the number and types of applications considered by VCAT. At the time of reporting, the result represents an improvement this year and Council continues to strive for effective decision-making in all planning matters.

Description: Kerbside collection bins missed
Variation: The number of missed bins has decreased over the 2023-24 year. Council contractors have been working to reduce the number of missed collections and are also refining  runs for efficiency.

Description: Cost of kerbside garbage bin collection service
Variation: The cost of waste collection has increased from last year. This is attributed to the increasing costs of the landfill levy, commodities and the consumer price index.

Description: Cost of kerbside recyclables collection service
Variation: The cost of the recycling bin and glass bin collection and processing has increased from last year. It is important to note that the City of Whiittlesea is one of the few Victorian Councils which has implemented the State Government requirement for glass bins and collection. This is attributed to the increasing costs of commodities and inflation. Tonnages collected have remained relatively stable despite an increase in tenements to last year. The container deposit scheme is likely to have contributed to the reduction in materials collected through the kerbside service. Over 3.5 million CDS containers have been collected via the four vending machines on Council managed land within the City of Whittlesea.

Description: Kerbside collection waste diverted from landfill
Variation: Across the four bins we have seen variation to the quantities collected across all streams. The quantity of landfill material has gone up, likely due to the increase in population. The quantity of recycling has decreased, likely due to the container deposit scheme impacts. The quantity of glass has gone up, as this is the first full year of service. The quantity of Food Organics and Garden Organics (FOGO) material has increased due to the increase in population and increase in the number of people opting into the service. However, the overall reduction in the diversion rate is considered to be primarily due to the introduction of the container deposit scheme, as this material is diverted from the kerbside system into the return collection points. Over 3.5 million CDS containers have been collected via the four vending machines on Council managed land within the City of Whittlesea.

Description: Expenses per property assessment
Variation: Our expenses per property assessment have increased mainly due to an increase in employee expenses and net loss on write-off of property, Infrastructure, plant and equipment. This indicator is projected to decrease in future year primarily because expenses are not rising significantly, while property assessments are experiencing growth.

Description: Average rate per property assessment
Variation: Our average rate per property assessment has increased due to a minimal rate increase applied in line with the Victorian Government's fair go rates system.

Description: Current assets compared to current liabilities
Variation: During 2023-24 current liabilities increased primarily due to increase in trust funds and deposits relating to the fire service levy at 30 June 2024. This is expected to decrease in line with Council's budget.

Description: Unrestricted cash compared to current liabilities
Variation: The definition of unrestricted cash subtracts cash and equivalents from current restrictions (primarily trust funds, statutory reserves and grants received in advance) but importantly does not include $265 million of term deposits classified as other financial assets in 2023-24. Under this definition, we exceed our available cash on hand, however we have sufficient cash balance to meet these commitments.

Description: Loans and borrowings compared to rates
Variation: Council did not draw down additional borrowings in the 2023-24 financial year. This indicator is forecast to increase in future years due to planned borrowings to fund future infrastructure investment.

Description: Loans and borrowings repayments compared to rates
Variation: The ratio decreased from 2022-23 primarily due to repayment of loans and borrowings, whilst rate revenue increased in line with the rate cap. The indicator is forecast to increase in future years in line with our expected borrowings to fund future infrastructure investment.

Description: Non-current liabilities compared to own source revenue
Variation: Council has not drawn down on additional loans the 2023-24 financial year, resulting in a decrease in non-current liabilities. The indicator is forecast to increase in future years in line with our expected borrowings to fund future infrastructure investment.

Description: Asset renewal and upgrade compared to depreciation
Variation: The ratio has increased compared to prior year due to higher renewal and upgrade expenditure undertaken compared to depreciation. Outer years forecast more moderate levels of capital works expenditure which is driven by the level of funding allocated to asset renewals and upgrades as part of the planning and budgeting process and priorities based on asset condition.

Description: Adjusted underlying surplus (or deficit)
Variation: The adjusted underlying deficit has increased primarily due to the timing of the 2024-25 Financial Assistance Grant payments as in prior financial years a significant portion was paid a year in advance. Additionally, employee costs has increased due to increased workcover levy, redundancy payments, and an increase in employee payments in line with the new Enterprise Bargaining Agreement. Future years' projections are expected to improve with income levels anticipated to increase at a greater level than expenditure.

Description: Rates compared to adjusted underlying revenue
Variation: Council continues to ensure rating levels are based on the community’s capacity to pay and within the State Government rate cap limits. This result remains within the expected range.

Variation:
This indicator is lower than target due to heavy investment over the previous three years. The four-year average is 108% and well above the target.

A number of projects listed in the adopted budget proved undeliverable due to cost escalations as a result of inflation and unprecedented construction cost increases.

In addition, the expansion of existing assets to meet growth demands have been categorised as new capital dollars. The expansion of parks, pedestrian and cycling infrastructure on existing assets can be considered as upgrade for the purposes of LGPRF reporting.
